mcp.title: MCP server
mcp.description: Control LogviewR's MCP (Model Context Protocol) server: enable/disable, status, audit log, and detected active threats.

overview.enabledDesc: Allows the external MCP process (launched by your Claude Code/Desktop client) to run tools against LogviewR. Disabling takes effect immediately, without restarting the process.
overview.architectureNote: The MCP process is started by your MCP client (Claude Code/Desktop), not by LogviewR. This panel cannot start or stop the process, only allow or block it.
overview.enableGuideIntro: MCP is disabled by default: once enabled, an AI agent (Claude Code/Desktop) can inspect fail2ban state, search your logs, and, with explicit confirmation, ban/unban IPs or start/stop jails. Enable it only if you intend to control LogviewR through an agent.
overview.enableGuideSteps: To integrate: add a "logviewr" entry to your MCP client's config (claude_desktop_config.json or .claude.json), pointing "command" at "npm run mcp:stdio" with "cwd" set to this repository's root, then restart your MCP client. This toggle only grants permission, it does not start the process itself.
overview.enableGuideDocLink: Full setup instructions and the tool list are in Docs/MCP_SERVER.md.

info.tagline: Real-time log visualization. Reads local log files from your machine or container ,no outgoing connection to servers.
info.aboutDescription: LogviewR is a web application to view and analyze log files in real time. It reads local log files from your machine or container (Apache, Nginx, Nginx Proxy Manager, system). No outgoing connection to your server, your logs stay on your infrastructure, which is better for security. Displays logs with search, filters and themes. config.logHistoryBody:
Number of log lines stored per IP and per jail in the fail2ban database.

Default: 10

Used by: fail2ban-client get <jail> banip <ip> matches

Recommendations:
• 10 = default (sufficient for diagnosis)
• 20–50 = good compromise for more context
• >100 = not recommended except for debug use, increases DB size

Change only if you need more log history per banned IP.
config.dbPurgeBody:
How long fail2ban keeps bans in its SQLite database.

Default: 86400 (1 day)

Recommendations:
• 86400 = 1 day (default — ok for normal use)
• 604800 = 7 days (good balance)
• 2592000 = 30 days (long history)
• 0 = disabled (keeps everything, risk of unlimited growth)

Increase if you want to see older bans in LogviewR. Do not exceed 90 days without monitoring DB size.

aide.countersTitle: Active bans vs Tracker vs Total cumulative
aide.countersText1: The dashboard displays several counters that measure different things — they are not meant to be identical.
aide.countersText2: 🔴 Active bans (header) — IPs currently in jail whose ban has not yet expired. Source: fail2ban real-time socket. Decreases when a ban expires.
aide.countersText3: 🟠 Tracker IPs (nav badge) — unique IPs that have had at least one ban since the internal history started (f2b_events). Includes expired bans. Only grows.
aide.countersText4: 🟣 Total cumulative bans (header) — Sum of all ban events recorded since installation. One IP can be counted several times.
aide.countersNote: The internal history (f2b_events) is kept indefinitely in dashboard.db — even if fail2ban purges its own DB according to dbpurgeage.
aide.logicTitle: fail2ban + ipset logic — attempts after ban
aide.logicText1: A tracker can show 15 attempts on an IP already in an ipset. That is normal — here is why.
aide.logicNote1: The ipset operates at kernel level, before the packet reaches the daemon. Fail2ban only sees the logs — it cannot block what the kernel has not yet intercepted.
aide.logicNote2: BANNED badge + IPSet on an IP with 15 attempts = coherent and correct. Attempts = history before the ban. IPSet = current state, no more attempts possible.
aide.logicWarn: If new attempts appear after adding to the ipset → config problem: badly positioned iptables rule, or log generated before the kernel DROP.
aide.localText1: fail2ban.local configures the global daemon: loglevel, logtarget, dbfile, dbpurgeage, dbmaxmatches.
aide.localText2: jail.local configures the jails: enabled, bantime, findtime, maxretry, filter, action, logpath.
aide.localNote: .conf vs .local rule: the .conf files are provided by the package (never edit them). The .local files are your overrides — only put what you want to change.

aide.fwCmdsWarn: iptables -F flushes ALL chains without confirmation — dangerous on a remote server without a backup SSH rule.

aide.safeNote: Banning these ranges would block legitimate traffic or break services (CDN proxy, DNS resolvers, SEO crawlers, monitoring). Add them to the ignoreip of your jails.
aide.providerCloudflareProxyDesc: If your domain is behind Cloudflare, all traffic passes through these IPs — banning them blocks everyone

aide.providerLetsEncryptDesc: ACME validation for SSL renewal — ban = broken certificates
aide.providerUptimeRobotDesc: Uptime monitoring — ban = false down alerts
aide.publicIpsText1: A ban on these ranges is often legitimate (bot/abuse from CDN or cloud). Informative reference — these IPs belong to recognized providers. Click a CIDR to copy it.
aide.providerCloudflareDesc: Global CDN — legitimate bots and frequent abuse
aide.providerAwsDesc: Public cloud — frequent source of scans
aide.regionalWarn: These ranges are statistically overrepresented in scan/brute-force logs. A preventive ban reduces the noise. Use according to your context — some may host legitimate users.
aide.providerChinaDesc: Main APNIC ranges — mass scans, SSH/HTTP brute-force
aide.providerRussiaDesc: RIPE NCC ranges — botnets, ransomware, phishing
aide.regionalNote: Source: APNIC, RIPE NCC, ARIN — public data. These ranges evolve — check regularly via whois or the RIRs.
